# Research Memorandum: Implementable Cognitive Mechanisms in *Learnability and Cognition*, File Pages 465 through 509

## Scope and Extraction Status

This section is almost entirely apparatus rather than argument. File pages 465 through 475 are the endnotes to chapters 4 through 7. File pages 476 through 495 are the reference list. File pages 496 through 509 are the index. There is no new body text advancing Pinker's theory here. I have not cited beyond file page 509. Because the section is apparatus, I will not pad it with inferred arguments; instead I will extract what the notes genuinely contribute to implementable mechanisms, flag what the apparatus cannot establish, and use the index only as a map of where earlier claims were made, never as evidence for those claims.

## What the Notes Actually Contribute

The most valuable material for my job is in the notes, which contain qualifications and micro-analyses that the main text compressed. Note 4 at file page 465 is a direct warning against a tempting engineering shortcut. Pinker, agreeing with Maratsos, doubts that motivated categories can be grasped by all speakers; motivations may be diachronically real yet opaque to a given generation, and judgments of well-formedness are often more discriminating than the best motivation a theorist can discover. He adds that motivations cannot be predicted in advance, so motivated classes must be learned as lists at least part of the time. For a machine, this blocks any design in which a similarity metric over semantic trees automatically generates the right classes. My proposal is that the machine store class membership as explicit listed data alongside any derived similarity structure, and that the listed data take precedence when they conflict with a computed motivation. Pinker states the doubt; the precedence rule is mine.

Note 5 at file page 465 gives a concrete case of semantic decomposition that a machine could store and match. Verbs like *butter*, *reward*, *credit*, and *supply* incorporate a theme that can be paraphrased as causing a substance or object to go to or onto a target, and they take optional *with*-objects whose semantics must add nonredundant information. The test cases are explicit: *He buttered the bread with butter* and *He rewarded her with a reward* are degraded because the *with*-object repeats the incorporated nominal. An implementable representation would store, for each such verb, a semantic tree containing a cause relation, a motion or transfer relation, and a theme node whose content is fixed by the verb root, plus a constraint that any *with*-argument must contribute a node not already present in the tree. The operation is a redundancy check over shared subtrees. The paraphrase relation and the redundancy constraint are Pinker's; the tree representation and the check are my engineering specification.

Note 8 at file pages 465 through 466 is a worked example of how a machine must handle lexical ambiguity in the input rather than assume clean categories. Food-preparation verbs like *pour*, *boil*, and *fry* appear to be counterexamples to a creation requirement in the double-object construction, but Pinker argues the food terms are ambiguous between raw material and consumable product, and the verbs entail creation of the edible product before giving. He supports this with distributional tests: *Can you pour me a cup of coffee* is better than *Can you pour me that coffee*, and *She cooked me some pork* is better than *She cooked me a pig*. For a machine, this means the semantic analyzer must represent a single object as having multiple type nodes, and the double-object rule must match against the consumable-product node rather than the raw-material node. The ambiguity analysis is Pinker's; the multi-type node representation is mine.

Note 12 at file page 466 is a case where the source itself flags an unresolved classification. *Sprinkle* is borderline between two classes: downward applied force meets one class criterion, force causing motion in a spatial distribution along a trajectory meets another, and the involvement of force seems to allow the alternation, while the similar verb *shake* is confined to one class. Pinker offers two possible causes and explicitly declines to explore a third involving phonological similarity to *spatter*, *splash*, and related forms. This is a genuine open problem for any class-learning algorithm, and I will not pretend the source resolves it.

Note 14 at file pages 466 through 467 supplies a naturalistic example of a speaker inventing a locative verb and stating the geometric principle governing the choice of form: cereal *ribboned into* the custard as a distinct separate area, versus being mixed throughout. This is direct evidence that the content-versus-container choice tracks the geometry of distribution, and it is the kind of data a learning machine would need as input.

Note 20 at file pages 467 through 468 lists positive exceptions that must be learned itemwise: *rattle* only by shaking, *leak* of secrets but not water, *bleed* of pipes but not clothing, *smoke* of cigarettes and ham but not firewood or butter, and transitive *shine* restricted to polish or direct a beam. Note 21 at file pages 468 adds that anticausativization applies only to causative verbs that could have been formed by a causativization rule to begin with, with no lexical specification of direction, manner of causation, or instrument motion. Together these define a machine requirement: the lexicon must carry per-item idiosyncratic restrictions that override any general rule, and the rule applicability test must inspect whether the verb's semantic tree already specifies the very parameters the rule would add.

Note 25 at file pages 468 through 469 raises a representational problem relevant to temporal processing. Pinker suggests that aspectual operations such as the progressive apply to the temporal properties of the role played by the surface subject, which is why instantaneous state-change verbs resist the progressive passive (*The balloon was being burst* is degraded). For a machine, this implies that the semantic record for each argument role must carry its own temporal profile, not just the event as a whole, and that aspectual operators must be able to select which role's timeline they zoom into. The role-indexed temporal profile is my proposal; the observation is Pinker's.

Note 3 at file page 472 states explicitly that broad-range and narrow-range rules include aspectual or time-line representation, perhaps with only a coarse point versus region distinction for the former. This is the closest the section comes to specifying temporal data structures, and it is a specification of content, not of storage or retrieval mechanism.

Note 5 at file pages 472 through 473 is important for grounding. Pinker argues that geometric and material properties of locative verbs must be attached to the theme argument in the motion structure rather than the patient in the action structure, because the properties of an object loaded into a container are interdependent with the container's shape, and the liquidity of sprayed stuff is intimately related to the shape it assumes while moving. He states this constraint is necessary for the learning account to work. This is a claim about where causal and informational grounding must be represented: the machine must bind object properties to the moving participant, not to the acted-upon participant, or the cross-situational generalization will fail.

Note 6 at file page 473 flags a possible problem case. For the *stuff* verbs, the two forms may be related not by copying identical structures but by a cognitive inference from resistance during insertion to overfullness of the container. If so, the rule-creation process would have to include not only coindexed parts but also the premises needed to infer the second structure. This is an explicit acknowledgment that some alternations may require inferential bridging rather than structural identity, and it is unresolved in the source.

Note 4 at file page 472 raises a sampling problem: verbs heard in both forms of an alternation may not be a random sample of the class, and nonwitnessed verbs may have more complex definitions. Pinker notes that a clustering procedure could exclude them if any legitimate semantic structure statistically correlates with the sample. This is a real obstacle for any learning machine operating on finite input, and the source offers a possibility rather than a solution.

## What the Apparatus Cannot Establish

The reference list and index confirm the scope of the theory but add no mechanisms. The index entries for event-category labeling, semantic structure hypothesis testing, broad and narrow conflation classes, linking rules, and the semantic bootstrapping hypothesis point back to chapters already covered by earlier readers; I will not restate those claims as if they were evidenced here. The index entry for clustering algorithms at file page 498 and the reference to Michalski and Stepp on conceptual clustering at file page 489 show that Pinker was aware of machine learning methods of his era, but the notes do not develop an algorithm. Nothing in this section addresses goals, planning, or action selection beyond the semantic representation of agent, patient, and causation; those remain outside what these pages support.

## Implications for the Thinking-Machine Design

My engineering proposals, clearly separated from Pinker's claims, are as follows. The machine should maintain a lexicon in which each entry holds a typed semantic tree, a set of listed idiosyncratic restrictions, and a set of candidate nodes subject to elimination by counterexample. Class membership should be stored explicitly and treated as authoritative over computed similarity. Argument roles should carry individual temporal profiles so that aspectual operations can target a specific participant. Object properties relevant to motion and containment should be bound to the theme node. Redundancy checks should govern the insertion of oblique arguments. Ambiguous input objects should be represented with multiple type nodes so that rules can match the appropriate construal. Rule applicability should be tested against the existing content of the verb's semantic tree to prevent double specification. None of these mechanisms is demonstrated to produce thought; they are data structures and operations that could run.

## Unresolved Questions

The notes leave several problems open that the next reader or another section must address. First, how does the machine decide class membership for borderline cases like *sprinkle*, where two criteria conflict and the source offers competing explanations without resolution. Second, how does the machine perform the inferential bridging required for verbs whose two forms are related by a cognitive inference rather than shared structure, as note 6 at file page 473 suggests for the *stuff* verbs. Third, how does the machine handle nonrandom sampling of input so that unseen verbs are not wrongly excluded from productive classes, a problem note 4 at file page 472 raises but does not solve. Fourth, what retrieval mechanism supports the cross-situational memory that the earlier chapters required and that these notes assume but never specify. Fifth, since this section is apparatus, the relationship between semantic structure and conceptual structure, and any mechanism for grounding abstract thought in spatial schemas, must be sought in the body chapters already covered or in *How the Mind Works*, not here.
